content: 1. Fluconazole has a slower rate and takes longer to achieve clearance of fungal infections in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compared to amphotericin B. This observation applies to all age groups, including individuals who have previously received antiretroviral therapy (ART) and develop cryptococcal meningitis after ART failure, as well as those restarting ART after an interruption. 2. For ART-experienced individuals, the consensus is to delay switching ART regimens for four weeks after completing an amphotericin B-based induction regimen or for 4–6 weeks after a fluconazole-based induction regimen. This recommendation is based on expert opinion due to the lack of clear prospective data. 3. There is no prospective evidence to guide the timing of ART initiation in asymptomatic individuals with cryptococcal antigenemia who have started pre-emptive antifungal therapy. However, guidelines from the Southern African HIV Clinicians’ Society suggest starting ART two weeks after initiating fluconazole. Immediate ART initiation may be considered if lumbar puncture excludes cryptococcal meningitis in individuals testing positive for whole-blood cryptococcal antigen. 4. ART-experienced individuals with cryptococcal meningitis should be evaluated for potential ART treatment failure, ideally confirmed with an HIV viral load test. ART switches should be deferred for four weeks after an amphotericin B-based induction regimen or 4–6 weeks after a fluconazole-based induction regimen. 5. Discontinuation of fluconazole maintenance therapy (secondary prophylaxis) is recommended for adults, adolescents, and children older than five years living with HIV who have successfully treated cryptococcal disease. This is contingent on being stable on ART and antifungal maintenance therapy for at least one year, with a CD4 count ≥100 cells/mm³ and a fully suppressed viral load if viral load monitoring is available. If viral load monitoring is unavailable, a CD4 count ≥200 cells/mm³ is required. 6. For children aged 2–5 years with successfully treated cryptococcal disease, antifungal maintenance therapy can be discontinued if they are stable on ART and antifungal therapy for at least one year, with a CD4 percentage >25% or an absolute count >750 cells/mm³. Maintenance therapy should not be discontinued for children younger than two years. 7. Secondary prophylaxis for cryptococcal disease should be restarted if the CD4 count drops below 100 cells/mm³ for adults, adolescents, and children older than five years, or below 25% or 750 cells/mm³ for children aged 2–5 years. Prophylaxis should also be restarted if a WHO stage 4 clinical event occurs, regardless of age. 8. CD4 count monitoring, while no longer recommended for ART response in settings with viral load testing, remains critical for decisions on discontinuing fluconazole maintenance therapy. Few studies have evaluated the risk of recurrent disease after discontinuing maintenance therapy, but available data suggest a very low risk of recurrence when individuals have completed initial antifungal therapy and achieved sustained immune recovery on ART. 9. A higher CD4 threshold (>200 cells/mm³) for discontinuing prophylaxis is recommended in settings with limited access to viral load testing and CD4 monitoring, as well as widespread use of less effective fluconazole monotherapy. In settings with viral load monitoring, discontinuation at a lower CD4 threshold (>100 cells/mm³) is advised if viral suppression is confirmed. 10. Optimal timing for discontinuing maintenance therapy in individuals with localized non-meningeal cryptococcal disease or isolated serum cryptococcal antigen positivity remains undetermined. Limited data exist for adolescents and children, but the same principles of sustained immune recovery on ART should apply. 11. A feasibility assessment conducted in 16 countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America identified significant barriers to diagnosing and treating cryptococcal disease. These include limited access to rapid diagnostics, optimal antifungal treatments, and tools for monitoring amphotericin B toxicity, as well as inadequate training of healthcare providers. 12. Rapid cryptococcal antigen tests, such as lateral flow assays, are often unavailable or prohibitively expensive. In many countries, India ink remains the primary diagnostic test, with turnaround times ranging from hours to days. Access to essential medications like amphotericin B and flucytosine is limited due to high costs, stock-outs, and poor forecasting. 13. In lowand middle-income countries, fluconazole monotherapy is commonly used without managing raised intracranial pressure, leading to unacceptably high mortality rates. Advocacy is needed to reduce the cost of flucytosine and simplify drug registration procedures. 14. Education and training gaps among healthcare providers contribute to suboptimal management of cryptococcal meningitis, including failure to diagnose and manage complications like raised intracranial pressure. Efforts should focus on improving provider education and national policy guidance. 15. Effective implementation of guidelines requires supportive supervision systems, prescribing decision-making aids, and national-level policy guidance. Dissemination strategies include presenting recommendations at international conferences, conducting workshops for country adaptation, and developing tools to assist resource-limited settings in prioritizing implementation. 16. The guidelines for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals will be launched as a web-based product and incorporated into the next update of the WHO consolidated ARV guidelines. These updates will be reviewed every 2–3 years to reflect changes in evidence and user needs.
